_comment: PROD sizing for Dispatch. Durable, always-warm, and expensive in the places where being
cheap costs more than the saving.
Same template, same modules, same resource shapes. Every difference from dev is in this
file, which is the property the whole exercise tests: if prod needed a different main.bicep,
then dev was never a rehearsal for anything.
SAME REGION as dev, and it should not be. Prod belongs in its own region - sharing one means
a regional outage takes dev and prod together, so the environment meant to rehearse a
recovery is gone at exactly the moment it is needed. It is here anyway because this
subscription permits ONE Container Apps environment in total, not one per region.
_sql: PROVISIONED, not serverless, and General Purpose rather than Day 23's S1.
Day 23 asked for S1 with zoneRedundant: true and what-if accepted it. That combination
cannot deploy: zone redundancy is unsupported on the DTU-based Standard tier, and what-if
validates template SHAPE, not whether a SKU supports the features requested alongside it.
The template was provably plannable and would still have failed on contact with ARM. It is
the clearest thing preparing an actual deployment surfaced.
GP_Gen5_2 is the smallest vCore SKU that supports zone redundancy. It is modest and
deliberately so: the right SKU is unknowable until real traffic exists. What matters is that
changing it is a one-line edit to this file rather than a redesign.
35 days is the Azure maximum for short-term retention. Point-in-time restore across five
weeks covers 'the corruption started before anyone noticed', which is the case that actually
_zoneRedundancy: FALSE, and it should be TRUE. This is a subscription limitation, not a design decision, and
it is the second one this capstone has hit - Day 23 recorded the same shape of problem with
The first prod deployment asked for zoneRedundant: true on GP_Gen5_2 and ARM refused:
ProvisioningDisabled: Provisioning of zone redundant database/pool is not supported
That message names neither the region nor the SKU, so both were checked directly rather
than guessed at. Both support it:
az account list-locations  -> centralindia reports availability zones 1, 2, 3
az sql db list-editions    -> GP_Gen5_2 reports zoneRedundant=True, status=Default
So the template is correct and the subscription is the constraint: an Azure for Students
offer does not permit zone-redundant provisioning. On a pay-as-you-go subscription this
line becomes true and nothing else in the template changes.
What is actually lost is worth stating plainly rather than filing as a footnote. Without
zone redundancy a single datacentre failure takes the production database down, and the
backup storage below drops from zone-redundant to locally-redundant with it - so the
recovery path shares a failure domain with the thing it is meant to recover.
_serviceBus: PREMIUM, and not for throughput. Premium buys three things Standard cannot: dedicated
resources so a noisy neighbour cannot affect latency, zone redundancy, and a predictable
cost instead of per-operation billing that scales with a bug. Standard would work and would
be defensible for a low-volume service; the reason it is not chosen is the first of those
three - on Standard, tail latency is somebody else's traffic.
Ten deliveries against dev's three. A production consumer failing is far more likely to be a
transient downstream outage than a poison message, and burning the retry budget in thirty
seconds turns a recoverable blip into a DLQ a human has to drain. P14D is long enough that a
subscription broken over a public holiday still has its messages when somebody returns.
_api: Four times the CPU, and NEVER fewer than two replicas. minReplicas 2, not 1: one replica
means every deployment, every node drain and every crash is a total outage for as long as
the replacement takes to start. Two is the smallest number that makes a rolling restart
invisible, and it is the difference between 'we deploy at 2am' and 'we deploy whenever'.
_observability: 90 days, and a much higher cap. Thirty days is fine for 'why did the build fail'. Ninety is
the floor for 'this started degrading gradually and nobody noticed for a month', which is
the incident telemetry is actually for. The cap is raised rather than removed: uncapped
